chunks: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Hammad ibn 'Isa, from 'Imran al-Halabi, from Abi 'Abd Allah عليه السلام, who said:
Whoever buys a sacrificial animal and does not know that it has a defect until he has paid its price, then comes to know after paying the price, it suffices him.

So this report admits two possibilities: one of them is that his hady is not obligatory, for that is permissible for him according to what was detailed in the first report. The second is that this may be a concession for one who has already paid the price and is unable to recover it; in that case, it is permissible for him to suffice with it.

key_terms.أَجْزَأَهُ: it sufficed him and fulfilled the requirement
key_terms.رُخْصَةً: a legal concession or allowance under difficulty
key_terms.عَيْبًا: a defect or blemish that affects the animal
key_terms.نَقَدَ ثَمَنَهُ: he paid its price in full
key_terms.هَدْيًا: a sacrificial animal offered as hady in the context of hajj rites
key_terms.يَقْتَصِرَ عَلَيْهِ: to limit himself to it and treat it as sufficient

ai.seo_question: If someone buys a defective hady animal without knowing and discovers the defect only after payment, does it still count?
ai.summary: This report states that if a person purchases a sacrificial animal for hady and only discovers its defect after paying the price, it may still suffice. The accompanying explanation presents two juridical possibilities: either the hady was non-obligatory, or this is a specific concession for someone unable to recover the payment after discovering the defect.
